job.title: Gradient Descent: Stepping Down x Squared

plan.goal: Understand that gradient descent finds a minimum by repeatedly stepping opposite the slope, and see two steps worked out on f(x) = x squared.

scenes.learningPoint: Gradient descent finds a function's lowest point by repeatedly stepping opposite the slope, which means downhill.
scenes.visualIntent: Axes with the curve f(x) = x squared, sampled at 15 points from x = -3.5 to 3.5. A dot at x = 3 (height 9), a short tangent line there, and an arrow pointing downhill toward x = 0, labelled 'step opposite the slope'.
scenes.narrationSummary: Gradient descent finds the lowest point of a curve by repeatedly taking small steps downhill, opposite the slope.

facts.text: minimum of x squared is at x

scenes.learningPoint: Each step uses new x = x minus step size times slope, and the steps shrink as the slope flattens near the minimum.
scenes.visualIntent: Written rule: 'slope = 2x', 'new x = x − 0.25 × slope'. Line 1: 'x = 3, slope 6, new x = 3 − 1.5 = 1.5'. Line 2: 'x = 1.5, slope 3, new x = 1.5 − 0.75 = 0.75'. On the same curve, dots at x = 3, 1.5, 0.75 joined by arrows, heights 9, 2.25, 0.5625 labelled.
scenes.narrationSummary: For x squared, the slope is 2x. Starting at 3, slope 6; times step size 0.25 moves us to 1.5. Then slope 3 moves us to 0.75, approaching zero.

limitations: Uses a one-variable curve, x squared; real uses have many variables, but the step rule is the same.
The starting point 3 and step size 0.25 are illustrative numbers chosen to keep the arithmetic simple.
Only two steps are shown; the process continues until the steps become tiny.
